title: Interpreting Acoustic Risk: Integrating Field Ethology and Laboratory Neuroscience in Rodents
content: Rodents hear sounds that signal predators, distressed companions, social opportunity, orsafety, yet the same sound can evoke different responses across individuals and contexts.Field studies show how free-living rodents use alarm-call structure, heterospecific calls,and caller reliability; laboratory studies reveal the neural and experience-dependentprocesses that evaluate sound. We bring these literatures together from the receiver’sperspective, distinguishing acoustic discrimination from inferred threat, physiologicalarousal from action, and habituation from learning about reliability or timing. Parallelauditory, amygdala, and midbrain pathways help explain why these outcomes comeapart, although most causal circuit evidence comes from conditioned or synthetic soundsrather than natural calls. We propose a receiver-centered account of three recurringdemands: responding rapidly to salient acoustic events, learning what particular soundspredict, and selecting actions according to context and ecological costs. These demandscan interact across defensive, social, and safety-related responses without necessarilyrelying on the same neural pathways. Comparing laboratory rats and mice with field-studied sciurids, we identify where the evidence converges, where it remains incomplete,and which questions could most productively connect the two disciplines.
